final_answer:
The debate began with the pro-AI position that artificial intelligence is good for society because it automates routine tasks, makes work easier for students and professionals, improves everyday convenience, and increases productivity. It was also argued that AI improves health and quality of life, expands accessibility for people with disabilities, and can improve workplace safety.

The main objections raised by the opposing side were that AI harms the economic well-being of many people and businesses, poses dangerous privacy risks, and undermines critical thinking skills for students and adults. These objections were used to support the conclusion that AI is not good for society.

In response, the pro-AI side repeatedly defended the claim that AI improves health and quality of life, and used that to support the conclusion that AI is good for society. The accessibility argument was also defended successfully: AI can improve accessibility for people with disabilities, which can make everyday life more convenient for marginalized groups and thereby improve quality of life. Later, the safety argument was added, saying AI can improve workplace safety, which again supports better health and quality of life. When privacy risks were raised again, the response was to combine both sides of the issue: AI can improve health and quality of life while also posing privacy risks. This led to a more balanced conclusion that AI can have both benefits and risks.

What remains undecided is whether the benefits of AI outweigh its harms, and therefore whether AI is overall good for society or not. No final argument was justified, so neither side fully won. What is known from the discussion is that AI has clear potential benefits: convenience, productivity, accessibility, health improvements, and workplace safety. It also has clear potential harms: privacy risks, possible economic disruption, and possible effects on critical thinking. So the debate established that AI is socially significant in both positive and negative ways, but it did not settle the final judgment.
